event: Elsie wakes at first light in the attic. It is the twentieth. It is Midsummer.
She says it out loud to the sloping boards: Midsummer. The fluttery feeling is back, busier.
She kneels up at the round window. Moonpenny's bud is fatter. A thin line of white shows at its tip.
She tells Moonpenny happy Midsummer, and not to rush on her account.
The parcel with the lantern drawn on it is in the satchel by the door. She checks it anyway.
She digs in the plant crate for her shawl. It's under Captain, rolled up, smelling of mint.
It's her mother's old blue shawl. It has no sleeves at all. She thinks Cora will say so.

Elsie says she hardly slept either, for the flutter. Noor says hers isn't a flutter. It's a stone.

event: At noon the Honeycomb shuts. They climb to the attic. Tamsin leans Margery by the door.
Elsie opens the round window. Canal air comes in, smelling of water and birch leaves.
Tamsin looks at the narrow bed. She says she'll take the floor. Elsie says the floor has splinters.
Elsie lies down by the wall and pats the blanket. Tamsin stands a long moment. She lies down.
Tamsin lies on the very edge, on her back, stiff as a plank, her arms crossed on her chest.
Elsie says she'll fall off like that. She tugs Tamsin in by the jerkin until their shoulders touch.
Elsie turns on her side and tucks her head under Tamsin's chin, as she did on the Marigold.
Tamsin's heart thumps under Elsie's cheek, hard and fast. Elsie says it's going like a drum.
Tamsin says it's the stairs. Elsie says it was two flights. Tamsin says shut up and sleep.
Elsie laughs into her collarbone and shuts her eyes. Tamsin's arm comes round her, slowly.
Elsie falls asleep with Tamsin's palm flat on her bare back, between the halter's laces.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 92 → 93 (kindness: held while they nap)

event: Elsie wakes at five. Tamsin is awake, still holding her, looking up at the sloping boards.
Tamsin says she slept. A bit. She says it as if confessing. Her hand hasn't moved.

event: Elsie says she snored like a kettle. Tamsin says that was Elsie. Elsie says it wasn't.
Tamsin says Elsie has a crease on her cheek from the jerkin. She runs her thumb along it, slowly.
Tamsin sits up fast. She says, pies. She pulls on her boots and says she'll see her at the Steps.
From the round window Elsie watches her go along Thimble Canal, still in her birch crown.
Moonpenny's bud has opened a little in the warm afternoon. The white is a finger's width now.
Elsie ties on the blue shawl, puts her crown back over her clip, and shoulders the satchel.

event: On the Midsummer page of her notebook, under the little boat, she writes: ring first, think after.
At quarter past seven the Lantern Steps are crowded with folk holding paper lanterns, waiting.
Below, little boats push off from the steps by the hundred, a lantern lit in each.
Halfway down Ines sits in a ring of bare stone, small in her black lace, Biscuit on her shoulder.

memory.fact: On the Lantern Steps folk leave a ring of bare stone round Ines.

event: At dusk, exactly as she said, Cora comes down the steps, her brass lantern at her belt.
Cora looks at the shawl. She says it has no sleeves. Elsie says she said so. Cora shuts her eyes.
Cora looks at the birch crown in Elsie's hair a long moment. She says nothing about it.
The Mere goes violet. Elsie watches the waterfront for a long green coat. It isn't there yet.

memory.fact: On Midsummer night hundreds of small lantern boats ring the barge on the dark water.

event: Odile Marsh calls for the guard boats. Elsie stands on her toes, looking, looking.
Noor comes along the waterfront as the last light goes, hands in pockets. Folk step out of her way.
She stops on the top step. She looks down at eleven. She looks at Elsie. She comes down.
Odile says eleven rides at buoy eleven, off the north reed beds. The darkest side. Ring first.

memory.fact: Buoy eleven lies off the north reed beds, on the darkest side of the barge.

event: Ines whispers that she'll look for the pink. Elsie touches her crown and says she'll wave.
They get in: Tamsin, steady; Tilly, wobbling; Elsie, sitting down hard and laughing.
Cora steps in without a wobble and sits in the bow by the hooded lantern. She lights it.
Noor stands on the bottom step, looking at the boat. She breathes in. She steps into the stern.
The boat dips. It doesn't tip. Noor sits down at the very back, far from the lantern.

memory.fact: Noor will come on the Midsummer barge guard, sitting at the back, away from the lantern.
Noor will come on the Midsummer barge guard, sitting at the back, away from the lantern.

event: The mooring rope holds. The lantern burns. Noor looks at it a long moment, and looks away.
Tamsin rows. Elsie, beside her on the middle seat, takes one oar, and they pull it together.
By half past eight they ride at buoy eleven, by tall black reeds. The Mere is lit with boats.
Far off in the middle of the lights the festival barge glows under its gold canopy.
At ten, across the water, a woman begins to sing, huge and clear. The whole Mere goes quiet.
Elsie says that's Celestine, Amara's mother. She tells the dark, out loud: I'm not listening.
Tamsin hands round the pies. Elsie opens the tin of honey cakes and passes it down the boat.
Noor takes a cake. She says she's had four of these already. She eats it in two bites.
Elsie asks: they're on the water now. Will she take a share? Noor says, put it toward the house.
Tamsin chokes on her pie. She says that isn't how a share goes. Noor says it is now.
Noor says she'd like to know where her coin went. Somewhere with a door. Somewhere that stays.
Elsie climbs back over the seat and hugs her round the neck. The boat rocks. Noor says, the boat.
Noor doesn't hug back. Her gloved hand comes up and holds Elsie's wrist, tight.
Elsie goes back to her seat. In the bow Cora is rubbing her hands together over the lantern hood.
It's turned cold off the water. Cora's fingertips are white. She tucks them under her arms.
Elsie takes the brown paper parcel out of her satchel and holds it out to Cora over Tilly's knees.
Cora looks at the lantern drawn on the paper. She doesn't take it. Elsie says, it's for your hands.
Cora takes it. She unties the string with stiff fingers. The lavender falls into her lap.
She lifts out the grey gloves, palm to palm, and holds them in the lantern light without a word.
Elsie says they're the grey of her eyes. That's why she held the wool up to her face in the shop.
Cora puts them on, one and then the other. They fit to the knuckle. She flexes her long fingers.
She says, thank you, Fairweather. Her voice breaks on the name. She turns to face the reeds.
She tucks the lavender into the top buttonhole of her coat, where the harebell was.
Tilly looks from the gloves to Elsie, her mouth a small o. She doesn't say anything. She looks down.
Tamsin shifts closer on the seat until her hip is against Elsie's, warm through the skirt.
Celestine's song ends. Cheers and little bells come over the water from the lantern boats.
At eleven the singing stops. The lantern boats hush and wait for the next song. Elsie waits too.
Elsie looks at the gold canopy and thinks of Amara somewhere under it, in her gold gown.
Behind her Noor says, low and sharp: the reeds. Something moved. No lantern on it.
A long black punt slides out of the reeds without a sound. Four shapes. Muffled oars.
It glides toward the empty lantern boats tied along the mooring line beyond eleven.
Elsie doesn't think. She snatches the brass bell from under the seat and rings it with all she has.
The bell clangs out over the water. All across the Mere, faces turn north. Other bells answer.
The punt doesn't run. Two lantern boats are already cut loose, and there's a tow line on them.
Cora throws back the lantern's hood. White light floods the punt. Four men fling up their arms.
Tamsin rows straight at them, hard. Eleven leaps. Tilly hangs on to the side, shrieking.
The thieves pole for the reeds with their prizes. Their punt pole cracks clean in two.
The tow line snaps with a twang. The lantern boats drift free. The punt slews into the reeds.
It sticks fast in the mud. Cornered, one thief stands up in it with a long iron boathook.
Tamsin ships her oars and stands, Margery up. She puts herself between the boathook and Elsie.
Under Elsie's breastbone the thread to Tamsin goes hot. Tamsin's breath comes short and hard.
Elsie puts her hand flat on Tamsin's back. She says, Tamsin, I'm here. Stay here with me.
Tamsin comes back to herself along the thread. She doesn't go red. She tells him: drop it, or swim.
Tilly pulls a bang vial off her belt and throws it into the water beside the punt. Bang.
The punt rolls over. All four thieves go into the black water among the reeds.
Three wade off into the reeds, cursing. The fourth thrashes. He goes under. He can't swim.
Noor stands up in the stern. The boat sways. She takes Tilly's lucky vial out of her pocket.
She throws it. It lands by his hand. Elsie shouts: hold it round the middle! Don't panic!
He grabs it and bobs up, gasping, clinging to it with both arms, eyes huge in the lantern light.
Odile Marsh's boat comes rowing up with three more guard boats, bells going. They haul him in.
Odile looks at the cut boats, the stuck punt, the broken pole, the snapped line. She looks at Noor.
She says that pole was new this spring. Noor says flatly that things break near her.
Odile says then she wants Noor near every thief on the Mere. She tows the lantern boats home.
She calls back over the water: pay at dawn, at the Steps. Ring first. That was good ringing.
Noor sits down at the back. She looks at the lantern on its pole. It's burning, steady.
She says, very quietly, it didn't sink. Elsie says no, it didn't. Noor says it again.
Elsie reaches back and takes her gloved hand. Noor holds on, all the way this time.
In the bow Cora writes in her ledger, in her new gloves. Elsie leans to see. Cora lets her.
It reads: Midsummer barge guard. Thieves, four. Skills used, none.
Tamsin sits down hard beside Elsie, trembling. She says she didn't go red. She didn't.
Elsie says she knows; she felt it. She leans on Tamsin's shoulder. Tamsin's arm comes round.
From the barge, small and shaky, a second voice starts to sing. It wobbles. It steadies.
It's the barrow tune, low and wandering. Two notes from the new voice, two from Celestine.
Elsie's eyes fill. She turns her face to the reeds and says out loud: I'm not listening.
Tilly asks what she's not listening to. Elsie says nothing, a bowl, and wipes her eyes, smiling.
At midnight the first firework goes up from the barge's bow and bursts gold over the Mere.
Blue stars follow. Tilly shrieks that it's Powder Lane blue-star, she'd know that blue anywhere.
Tilly grabs Elsie's arm with both hands and holds it through every blue one, her face turned up.
Elsie looks round the boat: four faces lit gold, then blue, then gold. Her boat. All of them.
Noor is looking up, the gold light on her face. One corner of her mouth has gone soft.
Cora isn't watching the sky. Elsie catches her looking at her. Cora looks up, quickly, at the stars.
Elsie tells them all she loves them. Tamsin coughs. Tilly squeezes her arm. Noor says, I heard.
At one they tie up at the Lantern Steps. Ines is asleep sitting up on a step, Biscuit in her lap.
Ines wakes as they climb out. She whispers that she saw the pink. She saw the bell. Everyone did.
Noor sits by Ines on the step. Biscuit climbs out of Ines's lap into Noor's. Noor goes still.
Biscuit turns round three times on the green coat and lies down, purring with no throat.
Noor puts one gloved hand on his little white skull. She doesn't take it away again.
Tamsin hoists sleepy Tilly's bag and says she'll walk her to Pickle Row. She'll see Elsie at dawn.
Tamsin straightens Elsie's birch crown with one finger. She goes up the steps with Tilly.
Cora says she will walk Fairweather to Thimble Canal. It's on her way. It isn't on her way.
Elsie hugs Noor goodnight round the neck, Biscuit and all. Noor says, dawn, like a promise.
Elsie and Cora walk along the dark canals. The lanterns are burning low. Nobody else is about.
Cora walks with her gloved hands at her sides. Every few steps she looks down at them.
Elsie says it's tomorrow now, or today. She asks if Cora will tell her why. Like she said, perhaps.
Cora stops on the bridge over Thimble Canal. She looks down at the water a long time.
Cora says when Elsie was out on the dome she didn't think of the Accord, or her ledger.
She says she held Elsie's ankle and knew she'd go off the dome with her before she let go.
She says that is why she said don't do that again. Because she couldn't bear it. Not the threads.
Elsie's eyes fill. She says she understands. She'd hold on too. That's what friends do, isn't it?
Cora looks at her a long moment. She says, very quietly, yes. That is what friends do.
Elsie hugs her. Cora's gloved hands come up and hold on to her back. They hold a long time.
Cora lets go. She says, goodnight, Fairweather. Dawn. She goes back over the bridge.
In the attic the round window is full of low lantern light. Moonpenny has opened.
One white flower, pale as the moon, wide open on its stem. It smells faintly sweet in the dark.
Elsie kneels up on the bed and whispers to it: you waited for Midsummer. You did it. We all did.
She lies down with the birch crown still on. The thread to Tamsin is warm under her breastbone.
Below the round window the last lamplighter's boat poles home along Thimble Canal.
